newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Scandal fails to keep Russian minister from office.
newsitem.headline: Scandal fails to keep Russian minister from office.

text.p: Russian Justice Minister Valentin Kovalyov, allegedly filmed taking a sauna in a gangland nightclub, was working at his office on Monday despite Sunday's announcement that he was being suspended from his post.
"We have not received any instructions and the minister spent all day working as usual," a ministry spokesman said.

The weekly newspaper Sovershenno Sekretno (Top Secret) last week published grainy snaps taken from a video which it said showed Kovalyov relaxing with naked women in September 1995 in the sauna of a nightclub frequented by mafia gangsters.
Kovalyov, 53, who is a member of the Kremlin's top-level Security Council, asked President Boris Yeltsin on Saturday to take him off the job until he could clear his name.

Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin said on Sunday Kovalyov would be temporarily removed from his post and on Monday one of Chernomyrdin's deputies, Boris Nemtsov, said an investigation had been launched.
Asked about the allegations, Nemtsov said jokingly: "I prefer to wash in the sauna." But he backed Kovalyov's view that the article was an invasion of privacy.

"The state has no right to climb into bed with the people, it has absolutely no right, and one would hope it would be the same the other way around," said Nemstov, one of the young ministers leading the government's new reform drive.
Outspoken nationalist politician Vladimir Zhirinovsky, who boasts that he is a sex symbol, gave Kovalyov even more support.
"Isn't it abhorrent to peer through keyholes? So what if some washes in some sauna somewhere?" he said. "Kovalyov hasn't done any harm to anyone."

Such scandals are all but unknown in Russia and Justice Ministry sources told Interfax news agency on Monday that Kovalyov, who resigned from the post-Soviet Russian Communist party on his appointment as a minister in January 1995, was planning to sue the popular, racy newspaper.
"The minister believes that the publication violated his right to privacy," Interfax quoted the source as saying.
"If we allow hidden cameras to pursue us everywhere we will have to say goodbye to hopes of building a law-based society in this country."

The ministry spokesman said he knew nothing of Kovalyov's plans. Chernomyrdin has the authority to suspend ministers but the request was addressed to Yeltsin. Only the president can sack ministers outright.
Yeltsin arrived home on Monday from a world leaders' meeting in the United States. A presidential spokesman said he had no information whether Yeltsin approved of suspending Kovalyov.
